newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Le Pen fails to stop critical TV programme.
newsitem.headline: France's Le Pen fails to stop critical TV programme.

text.p: French state television on Thursday ran a documentary highly critical of far-rightist politician Jean-Marie Le Pen after a court rejected his bid to have excerpts of his speeches deleted from the programme.

The programme, "Le Pen in Quotes", used testimonies from historians and disgruntled former allies of Le Pen to draw parallels between his statements on immigrants and racial inequality with the ideology of the Nazis and of the French wartime collaborationist Vichy regime.

The one-hour programme on France-2 television also cited inconsistencies in Le Pen's statements on his personal history and wealth, producing testimonies purported to show that he had built up a large fortune from personal legacies of National Front sympathisers.

"This is a programme...intended only to damage Jean-Marie Le Pen's image, without ever allowing him to speak up in his defence, which is scandalous if not Stalinist," The National Front said in a statement.

A judge hours earlier turned down Le Pen's emergency request to have his speeches cut out from the programme on the grounds that they were his private "literary property" and could not be used without his permission.
Judge Jean-Jacques Gomez said he had turned down his plea on the grounds neither man had seen the documentary in question.

"This was a frightening document," Culture Minister Philippe Douste-Blazy said after the programme. He called on politicians, students and unionists to canvas and work against Le Pen or be guilty of "failing to assist a Republic in danger".

The programme was screened against a background of protests against a fiercely contested immigration bill to tighten up controls to prevent Third World citizens on short-term tourist visas from overstaying and working illegally in France.
It was aired as Le Pen held a rally in Paris' Left Bank Latin Quarter. Several hundred students demonstrated on nearby Sorbonne square against the rally and the bill.

Heavy riot police forces stopped them marching on the hall where Le Pen, who won 15 percent of the votes in the 1995 presidential election, was to deliver what was billed as a major speech on social policies.

The National Assembly's legislation committee passed on Thursday an amendment to the immigration bill aimed at rescuing Prime Minister Alain Juppe's conservative government from a torrent of protests by artists, intellectuals and students.

The bill would have required citizens to report to the police when a foreign guest left their home and some had compared it to the obligation to denounce the presence of Jews during the Nazi occupation of France.

The amendment makes government prefects rather than town mayors responsible for issuing "accommodation certificates" to foreigners subject to visa requirements. The foreigner himself would have to hand in the form to an immigration official on leaving the country.
Opponents of the bill accuse the government of borrowing from the policies of the anti-immigrant National Front in a bid to win back voters.
Major protests are scheduled in Paris on Saturday, and on Monday when the bill, already passed by the National Assembly and the Senate, returns to the lower house for a final reading.

Several French "Righteous" on Thursday condemned the stiffening of French immigration regulations as creating a worrying atmosphere and turning immigrants from Africa and Asia into second-class individuals.
The title of "Righteous among the Righteous" is given by Israel to people who rescued Jews from deportationn to Nazi death camps during World War Two.
